warmup.q: The bakery's program asks its old stock book how many loaves each of 10 shops has left. Each call blocks its thread for 100 ms. The code is Flux.fromIterable(shops).flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.loavesLeft(s))).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()). About how long does it take?
options: About 100 ms: flatMap runs them concurrently on boundedElastic threads
About 1 second: all ten run in turn on one boundedElastic thread
About 250 ms: boundedElastic has one thread per core
warmup.why: subscribeOn on the outer Flux moves the subscription to one boundedElastic thread. flatMap subscribes to each inner fromCallable on that same thread, and a fromCallable runs its call as it is subscribed, so the calls take turns. To get concurrency, put subscribeOn on each inner Mono. flatMap only subscribes to many inners at once; the threads have to come from the inners. The section on blocking calls measures all three versions.

opening:
Picture the bakery on a busy morning. A few workers keep the belts moving, and none of them ever stands still. Then someone puts a telephone at the slicing station, and the old stock room has to be called about every loaf. The stock room is in no hurry. While the worker at the slicer waits with the phone at her ear, every loaf on her belt waits too.

A Reactor program has the same workers, called threads, and the same phone, called a blocking call. The surprise is how few workers Reactor keeps: its main team has one per processor core. The easy trap is one line in the wrong place, which leaves a single worker making every call in turn.

In Errors, retries and timeouts, the pauses of a retry ran on a thread named parallel-1. In this lesson, we'll find out who those workers are and move work between them with publishOn and subscribeOn. Then we'll hand the slow calls to workers who are allowed to wait, and see why block() is refused on some threads. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a phone at the slicing station and a worker who couldn't put it down. Reactor's workers are threads, and by default the one that delivers a signal works every station after it. publishOn hands the belt to another team, subscribeOn says who starts the oven, and slow calls go to boundedElastic, one wrapped call per inner Mono.

Now search your own code for .block() inside a map or flatMap, and for a subscribeOn written after a flatMap of fromCallable calls.

Next, we'll come back to the packer's slip. publishOn quietly asked for 256 items at a time. Who writes the slips in real code, and what do we do with a source that can't read them?

sections.h: Who works each station: the thread that delivered the last signal
sections.html:
So far the belt has had stations but no workers. In a program, the workers are threads: paths of work that each run one piece of code at a time. An ExecutorService, the JDK object from the executors track, keeps its own team of threads. A Reactor chain doesn't. Unless you say otherwise, the source runs on the thread that called subscribe(). Each operator, each station on the belt, runs on the thread that delivered the signal to it, the item, error or completion that just arrived.

On the bakery line, the worker who puts a loaf on the belt carries it through every station to the end. ThreadTourDemo, in the Try it, shows it with Flux.range(1, 2).map(...).subscribe(...) called from main:

1. no scheduler anywhere
  source emits 1             on main
  subscriber gets 10         on main
  source emits 2             on main
  subscriber gets 20         on main

Every step ran on main, item by item, and subscribe returned only when the range was done.

Other threads appear when something asynchronous, something that finishes later on its own schedule, sits in the chain. A timer fires on one of Reactor's own threads, and Mono.delay, interval, delayElements, timeout and the pauses of Retry.backoff are all timers. The operators after the timer carry on there. A non-blocking client, one that hands its request to the operating system and moves on (Why reactive), delivers its answer on its own threads too. The demo's other two parts show the timers:

2. after a timer (Mono.delay)
  timer fires                on parallel-1
  map after the timer        on parallel-1
3. flatMap over three timers
  downstream gets 1          on parallel-2
  downstream gets 2          on parallel-3
  downstream gets 3          on parallel-4

The map after the timer ran on the timer's thread. In the flatMap over three timers, the items arrived on three different threads, but still one at a time. Rule 1.3 from Why reactive holds: signals to one subscriber never overlap, even when the thread changes.

When you want to choose the worker, you pass a scheduler, Reactor's source of threads. It is close to an ExecutorService, and it is also a clock, which is how a test can fake time. Reactor 3.8 has four shared ones, like four teams in the bakery:

Scheduler Threads Use it for
Schedulers.immediate() the current thread a placeholder that changes nothing
Schedulers.single() one shared thread cheap work that must stay in order
Schedulers.parallel() one per CPU core CPU work and timers; never block here
Schedulers.boundedElastic() up to 10 x cores, then a queue of 100,000 tasks blocking calls

A CPU core is the part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. So on a 4-core machine, parallel is a team of four quick hands who must never stand still. boundedElastic is a back room of up to forty workers who are allowed to wait on the phone.

The threads of parallel and single are marked as non-blocking, and Reactor refuses block() on them, as the last section shows. boundedElastic creates threads when it needs them, up to its cap, reuses them, and lets a worker go after 60 seconds with nothing to do. Past the cap, tasks wait in its queue. Past the queue, it throws RejectedExecutionException.

You can build your own with Schedulers.newParallel, newBoundedElastic or fromExecutorService, and you then have to dispose() them. The reference guide still mentions Schedulers.elastic(), which no longer exists in 3.8: use boundedElastic().

A Reactor chain runs on whatever thread delivered the last signal, unless you say otherwise.

So far a timer chose the thread for us. Next, we'll choose it ourselves.

try.title: A tour of the threads
steps: ThreadTourDemo prints the thread of each step in three chains: no scheduler at all, a chain after Mono.delay, and a flatMap over three timers. Predict each thread name before you run it.
In part 3, add .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) right before the doOnNext (and import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers). Predict the threads, then run it again.

code.title: ThreadTourDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** Where does each step run? Reactor stays on whatever thread delivered the last signal. */ public class ThreadTourDemo { static void where(String step) { System.out.printf(" %-26s on %s%n", step, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. no scheduler anywhere"); Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext(i -> where("source emits " + i)) .map(i -> i * 10) .subscribe(i -> where("subscriber gets " + i)); System.out.println("2. after a timer (Mono.delay)"); Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)) .doOnNext(t -> where("timer fires")) .map(t -> "ok") .doOnNext(v -> where("map after the timer")) .block(); System.out.println("3. flatMap over three timers"); Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10L * i)).thenReturn(i)) .doOnNext(i -> where("downstream gets " + i)) .blockLast(); } }

Reactor stays on whatever thread delivered the last signal. */ fun main() { println("1. no scheduler anywhere") Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext { i -> where("source emits $i") } .map { i -> i * 10 } .subscribe { i -> where("subscriber gets $i") } println("2. after a timer (Mono.delay)") Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)) .doOnNext { where("timer fires") } .map { "ok" } .doOnNext { where("map after the timer") } .block() println("3. flatMap over three timers") Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap { i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10L * i)).thenReturn(i) } .doOnNext { i -> where("downstream gets $i") } .blockLast() }

try.expect: Part 1 runs entirely on main, and the source and the subscriber take turns item by item. Part 2 runs on parallel-1, the timer's thread, including the map after it. Part 3 delivers the three items on three different parallel threads (for example parallel-2, parallel-3, parallel-4). After your change, all three arrive on single-1: a hand-over point moved them to one worker.

sections.h: publishOn moves what comes after it; subscribeOn moves the source
sections.html:
Two operators move work to another team, and they move different things.

publishOn(scheduler) sits on the belt itself, in the path of the data. Items arrive from above on whatever thread, and publishOn puts them in a queue (it asks for 256 at a time by default). Then one worker of the scheduler carries them on to the operators below. Everything after it, up to the next publishOn, runs on that worker. Everything before it is unaffected.

On the bakery line, publishOn is a hand-over point. Up to here, the oven's worker carries each loaf; from here on, a worker from another team does. Use it to get work off a thread that must stay free, or onto parallel for a step that keeps the processor busy.

subscribeOn(scheduler) sits on the path of the subscription instead. When you call subscribe(), Reactor passes the subscription up the chain from your end to the source, as Mono and Flux showed. subscribeOn makes that trip, and the request(n) calls after it, continue on the scheduler's thread. So the source starts producing there, and a source that does its work as it is subscribed, such as fromCallable or range, runs there.

In the bakery, subscribeOn is the line on the signed order form that says which team starts the oven, and it doesn't matter where on the form you write it:

Java
Flux.range(1, 1)
        .doOnNext(i -> where("source"))                 // boundedElastic-1
        .publishOn(Schedulers.single())
        .doOnNext(i -> where("after publishOn"))        // single-1
        .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())       // written last, still moves the source
        .blockLast();
Kotlin
Flux.range(1, 1)
    .doOnNext { where("source") }                       // boundedElastic-1
    .publishOn(Schedulers.single())
    .doOnNext { where("after publishOn") }              // single-1
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())           // written last, still moves the source
    .blockLast()

PublishSubscribeDemo, in the Try it, runs that chain:

2. subscribeOn(boundedElastic) written last
  source                 on boundedElastic-1
  after publishOn        on single-1

The source ran on boundedElastic-1, although subscribeOn was written last. After the hand-over point, the item moved to single-1. The figure below draws both paths.

With two subscribeOn calls, the one nearest the source wins. The other one only adds a thread hop on the way up. Here the order-form picture breaks: a real form with two lines that disagree would go back to the customer, while Reactor quietly obeys the line nearest the oven. The reference guide recommends writing subscribeOn right after the source, where a reader looks for it.

Two limits. If the source is asynchronous itself, such as Mono.delay or a non-blocking client, subscribeOn moves only the subscribe call, and the items still arrive on the source's own threads. And after a publishOn below the source, the data path belongs to the publishOn scheduler, as the second line of the output shows.

publishOn moves the operators after it. subscribeOn moves the source, wherever you write it.

Now we can decide where a slow call should run. First, let's look at what makes a call slow in the wrong way.

sections.h: A slow phone call at one station: wrap blocking calls for boundedElastic
sections.html:
The bakery keeps its stock in an old database, a program that stores data on disk and answers questions about it. The bakery's program reaches it through a blocking driver, a library that holds the calling thread until the database answers, like a worker waiting on the phone. stock.loavesLeft("shop-7") takes about 100 ms, and for all of that time its thread does nothing else. That's a blocking call. Reading a file with Files.readAllLines is one too, and so is any older client library that waits for its answers.

Run one on parallel, and you take one of its few workers off the belts. Four slow calls on a 4-core machine stop every timer and every other chain that shares that team. Reactor's FAQ gives the standard wrapper:

Java
Mono<Integer> loavesLeft(String shop) {
    return Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.loavesLeft(shop))     // lazy: runs per subscription
            .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());        // on a thread that may block
}
Kotlin
fun loavesLeft(shop: String): Mono<Int> =
    Mono.fromCallable { stock.loavesLeft(shop) }              // lazy: runs per subscription
        .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())             // on a thread that may block

fromCallable makes the call lazy and turns a thrown exception into onError (Mono and Flux). subscribeOn puts the call on a thread that is allowed to block. As the FAQ says, subscribeOn doesn't subscribe to anything. It only says where the work runs once somebody subscribes.

For many calls, the subscribeOn must sit on each inner Mono. This version looks concurrent:

Java
// Naive: looks concurrent, isn't
Flux.fromIterable(shops)
        .flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.loavesLeft(s)))
        .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());      // one thread makes every call, in turn
Kotlin
// Naive: looks concurrent, isn't
Flux.fromIterable(shops)
    .flatMap { s -> Mono.fromCallable { stock.loavesLeft(s) } }
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())           // one thread makes every call, in turn

flatMap subscribes to each inner on the thread it is running on, and a fromCallable runs right there, as it is subscribed. So the calls take turns on one thread. BlockingCallDemo, in the Try it, makes eight calls of 100 ms three ways:

1. fromCallable, no scheduler      8 calls in 893 ms on 1 thread(s), e.g. main (virtual=false)
2. subscribeOn on the outer Flux   8 calls in 813 ms on 1 thread(s), e.g. boundedElastic-1 (virtual=false)
3. subscribeOn on each call        8 calls in 116 ms on 8 thread(s), e.g. boundedElastic-4 (virtual=false)

The second line is the trap: eight calls, one worker, and a queue at the phone. With subscribeOn inside the flatMap, the same eight calls took 116 ms on eight threads, about seven times faster on this busy machine. Then cap them with flatMap's concurrency argument from Transforming streams, so that a stock database that allows 20 connections isn't asked for 40 at once.

A blocking call needs fromCallable and subscribeOn(boundedElastic) on its own Mono.

Since Reactor 3.6, boundedElastic can use virtual threads, the light threads from Part 1 that let go of their carrier thread while they wait. On JDK 21 or later, start the JVM with -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true, and the shared boundedElastic() runs every task on a new virtual thread, named loomBoundedElastic-N. The caps stay the same, and the Javadoc suggests raising reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticSize when you turn it on. The property is read once, when Reactor's Schedulers class loads, so put it on the command line. The virtual threads track applies here too: on JDK 21 to 23, a driver that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier.

Wrapping a call moves it off the wrong thread. The last trap is code that tries to wait in the middle of a chain.

try.title: Eight blocking calls, three ways
steps: BlockingCallDemo makes eight stock-book calls that each block for 100 ms: with no scheduler, with subscribeOn on the outer Flux, and with subscribeOn on each inner call. Predict the time and the number of threads for each.

Run it again with -Pargs=virtual added to the command. The demo then sets reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads before Reactor loads its schedulers. Look at the thread names and the virtual flag.

code.title: BlockingCallDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Eight blocking stock-book calls of 100 ms each. Where you put subscribeOn decides how long they take. */ public class BlockingCallDemo { static final Set<Thread> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); // a call through a blocking database driver: it holds the calling thread for 100 ms static int loavesLeft(String shop) { threads.add(Thread.currentThread()); try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 10; } static void run(String title, Flux<Integer> counts) { threads.clear(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long n = counts.count().block(); Thread one = threads.iterator().next(); System.out.printf("%-34s %d calls in %3d ms on %d thread(s), e.g. %s (virtual=%s)%n", title, n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size(), one.getName(), one.isVirtual()); } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("virtual")) { // must be set before Reactor's Schedulers class is first used; normally a -D JVM flag System.setProperty("reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads", "true"); } List<String> shops = List.of("shop-1", "shop-2", "shop-3", "shop-4", "shop-5", "shop-6", "shop-7", "shop-8"); run("1. fromCallable, no scheduler", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> loavesLeft(s)))); run("2. subscribeOn on the outer Flux", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> loavesLeft(s))) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())); run("3. subscribeOn on each call", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> loavesLeft(s)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()))); } }

alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l06 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap private val threads: MutableSet<Thread> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() // a call through a blocking database driver: it holds the calling thread for 100 ms private fun loavesLeft(shop: String): Int { threads += Thread.currentThread() Thread.sleep(100) return 10 } private fun run(title: String, counts: Flux<Int>) { threads.clear() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val n = counts.count().block() val one = threads.first() println("%-34s %d calls in %3d ms on %d thread(s), e.g. %s (virtual=%s)".format(title, n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size, one.name, one.isVirtual)) } /** Eight blocking stock-book calls of 100 ms each. Where you put subscribeOn decides how long they take. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "virtual") { // must be set before Reactor's Schedulers class is first used; normally a -D JVM flag System.setProperty("reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads", "true") } val shops = listOf("shop-1", "shop-2", "shop-3", "shop-4", "shop-5", "shop-6", "shop-7", "shop-8") run("1. fromCallable, no scheduler", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap { s -> Mono.fromCallable { loavesLeft(s) } }) run("2. subscribeOn on the outer Flux", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap { s -> Mono.fromCallable { loavesLeft(s) } } .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())) run("3. subscribeOn on each call", Flux.fromIterable(shops) .flatMap { s -> Mono.fromCallable { loavesLeft(s) }.subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) }) }

try.expect: No scheduler: about 800 ms on main (869 to 893 ms in runs here). subscribeOn outside: about 800 ms on one thread, boundedElastic-1. subscribeOn on each call: a little over 100 ms on 8 threads (115 to 125 ms here). With -Pargs=virtual, the thread names become loomBoundedElastic-N and virtual=true, with the same timings: virtual threads change the cost of each thread, not the shape of the chain.

sections.h: Keep block() at the edges of reactive code
sections.html:
block() subscribes and makes the calling thread wait until the Mono finishes, as Mono and Flux showed. On a parallel or single thread, that's a bug, and Reactor checks for it: block(), blockFirst(), blockLast(), toIterable() and toStream() all throw IllegalStateException there.

The bug shows up in code like the first line below, once the item comes from a timer, a timeout or a non-blocking client. The bakery wants to know what the loaves in a shop are worth, at the current price per loaf from its price list, a non-blocking client:

Java
loaves.map(n -> worth(n, prices.pricePerLoaf().block()))           // Naive: throws on a parallel thread
loaves.flatMap(n -> prices.pricePerLoaf().map(p -> worth(n, p)))    // composes instead
Kotlin
loaves.map { n -> worth(n, prices.pricePerLoaf().block()!!) }      // Naive: throws on a parallel thread
loaves.flatMap { n -> prices.pricePerLoaf().map { p -> worth(n, p) } }   // composes instead

BlockInParallelDemo, in the Try it, runs both lines, with the count of loaves arriving from a timer:

1. block() inside map:  block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread parallel-1
2. flatMap instead:     250.00

The flatMap version doesn't wait at all. It hands the price lookup to the chain and carries on when the price arrives: 100 loaves at 2.50 each.

The check is a safety net with holes in it. Mono.just(x).block() takes a shortcut for a value that is already there, and doesn't check the thread at all. So a unit test whose stubs return Mono.just passes, and the bug waits patiently for the real server. The check also only knows threads that carry Reactor's NonBlocking marker, a small interface that its own threads implement. A thread that some other library created isn't marked, so block() there works, and holds that thread until the answer comes.

To find the blocking calls that the check misses, the Reactor team has a separate tool, BlockHound (not in the labs). It's a Java agent, a library loaded when the JVM starts that changes classes as they load. It throws when a non-blocking thread calls something like Thread.sleep or a blocking read from the network.

So where is block() fine? In main, in a test (though StepVerifier is better), and at the edge where reactive code meets code that waits anyway, on a thread that is yours to block. On boundedElastic it's allowed, and it costs you one of a limited set of threads. Inside a chain, there is always an operator that composes instead: flatMap, zipWith or then.

Inside a chain, compose with flatMap. Keep block() for the edges.

That leaves one question for the place where most reactive code runs: a web server.

try.title: When block() is refused
steps: BlockInParallelDemo works out what 100 loaves are worth at the price per loaf, four ways: block() inside map, flatMap, block() on a Mono.just, and block() after publishOn(boundedElastic()). The count arrives from Mono.delay, so on a parallel thread. Predict which lines fail.
Change loaves to Mono.just(100) and run it again. Predict line 1 first.

code.title: BlockInParallelDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.time.Duration; /** block() on a Reactor parallel thread is refused. flatMap composes instead. */ public class BlockInParallelDemo { static Mono<BigDecimal> pricePerLoaf() { // a non-blocking price-list lookup return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(20)).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("2.50")); } static BigDecimal worth(int loaves, BigDecimal price) { return price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(loaves)); } public static void main(String[] args) { // a timer emits on a parallel thread, just as a non-blocking client delivers its answer on a Reactor thread Mono<Integer> loaves = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(100); try { loaves.map(n -> worth(n, pricePerLoaf().block())).block(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("1. block() inside map: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("2. flatMap instead: " + loaves.flatMap(n -> pricePerLoaf().map(p -> worth(n, p))).block()); System.out.println("3. Mono.just(..).block() inside map: " + loaves.map(n -> worth(n, Mono.just(new BigDecimal("2.50")).block())).block() + " (a shortcut, not a permission)"); System.out.println("4. block() after publishOn(boundedElastic): " + loaves.publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()).map(n -> worth(n, pricePerLoaf().block())).block()); } }

alt.title: BlockInParallelDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l06 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers import java.math.BigDecimal import java.time.Duration private fun pricePerLoaf(): Mono<BigDecimal> = // a non-blocking price-list lookup Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(20)).thenReturn(BigDecimal("2.50")) private fun worth(loaves: Int, price: BigDecimal): BigDecimal = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(loaves.toLong())) /** block() on a Reactor parallel thread is refused. flatMap composes instead. */ fun main() { // a timer emits on a parallel thread, just as a non-blocking client delivers its answer on a Reactor thread val loaves: Mono<Int> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(100) try { loaves.map { n -> worth(n, pricePerLoaf().block()!!) }.block() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("1. block() inside map: ${e.message}") } println("2. flatMap instead: " + loaves.flatMap { n -> pricePerLoaf().map { p -> worth(n, p) } }.block()) println("3. Mono.just(..).block() inside map: " + loaves.map { n -> worth(n, Mono.just(BigDecimal("2.50")).block()!!) }.block() + " (a shortcut, not a permission)") println("4. block() after publishOn(boundedElastic): " + loaves.publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()).map { n -> worth(n, pricePerLoaf().block()!!) }.block()) }

try.expect: Line 1 prints the block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread parallel-1 message. Lines 2, 3 and 4 print 250.00: flatMap composes, Mono.just takes its shortcut, and boundedElastic threads are allowed to block. With Mono.just(100) as the count, line 1 also prints 250.00, because map now runs on main. Same code, different thread, different result: that's why tests with Mono.just stubs miss this bug.

aside.title: Where do a web server's threads fit in?
aside.html: If you write web services, the server hands each request to your code on one of its own threads. A reactive server, such as the one under Spring WebFlux, uses a few event-loop threads, each serving many visitors without ever waiting (Why reactive). Those threads are marked non-blocking, so a block() there throws the same error, naming a thread such as reactor-http-nio-2. A blocking database call in a map throws nothing at all. It just stops every visitor that thread serves until the database answers, so wrap it exactly as the section on blocking calls shows.

compare.title: Choosing threads in Reactor and in coroutines

java.title: StockReport.java (Reactor)
java.html: // Reactor: say where each part of the chain runs Mono<Report> stockReport(String shop) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.linesFor(shop)) // blocking database call... .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // ...so the source runs here .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) // what follows runs here .map(lines -> report.render(lines)); // CPU-heavy page layout }

kotlin.title: StockReport.kt (coroutines)
kotlin.html: // Kotlin coroutines: switch the dispatcher around each block of work suspend fun stockReport(shop: String): Report { val lines = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { stock.linesFor(shop) } // blocking database call return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { report.render(lines) } // CPU-heavy page layout }

compare.note: Reactor attaches threads to positions in a chain: subscribeOn picks where the source runs and publishOn picks where the rest runs. Coroutines attach them to blocks of code: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) runs the block on the IO dispatcher, the coroutines' version of a scheduler, and comes back afterwards, so you read the thread switches from top to bottom. The pools line up: Dispatchers.Default has one thread per core like parallel, and Dispatchers.IO is for blocking calls like boundedElastic. Kotlin Flow has one more twist: flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) changes where everything above it runs, which is closer to subscribeOn than to publishOn. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges the two worlds with Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher().

worked.title: Get a blocking lookup off the server's thread

steps.say: The bakery's website has a page that shows the status of a cake order. The web server hands each request to this method as a Mono, and the method looks the order up in the old order database through orders, a repository (a class that wraps the database calls) that blocks. When the shop is busy, every page on the website slows down, not just this one. Find the cause before you read on.
steps.code: Mono<OrderView> view(Mono<OrderRequest> request) { return request .map(req -> orders.find(req.orderId())) // blocking database call, about 30 ms .map(OrderView::from); }

alt.html: fun view(request: Mono<OrderRequest>): Mono<OrderView> = request .map { req -> orders.find(req.orderId) } // blocking database call, about 30 ms .map(OrderView::from)

steps.say: The request arrives on one of the server's few event-loop threads, the threads that serve many visitors without waiting, and map runs on whatever thread delivered the item. So the 30 ms database call runs on the event loop. While it waits for the database, every other visitor that loop serves waits too. Nothing throws, because a database call isn't a block(), and a unit test with Mono.just(request) runs it on the test thread, where it looks fine.

Turn the lookup into its own inner Mono, wrapped and moved off the server's thread. The map after it now runs on the boundedElastic thread that finished the lookup, which is fine for a cheap conversion. A heavy step would get a publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) first.
steps.code: Mono<OrderView> view(Mono<OrderRequest> request) { return request .flatMap(req -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> orders.find(req.orderId())) // 1. wrap the blocking call .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())) // 2. run it off the server's thread .map(OrderView::from); // 3. continues on boundedElastic }

alt.html: fun view(request: Mono<OrderRequest>): Mono<OrderView> = request .flatMap { req -> Mono.fromCallable { orders.find(req.orderId) } // 1. wrap the blocking call .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. run it off the server's thread } .map(OrderView::from) // 3. continues on boundedElastic

steps.say: Pin it with a test. The trick is to make the request arrive on a non-blocking thread, as it does in production, and to record the thread the repository sees.
steps.code: @Test void lookupRunsOnBoundedElastic() { AtomicReference<String> thread = new AtomicReference<>(); orders.onFind(() -> thread.set(Thread.currentThread().getName())); Mono<OrderRequest> request = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(5)) // 4. arrive on a non-blocking thread, .thenReturn(new OrderRequest("order-42")); // as the real server does StepVerifier.create(page.view(request)).expectNextCount(1).verifyComplete(); assertThat(thread.get()).startsWith("boundedElastic-"); }

alt.html: @Test fun `lookup runs on boundedElastic`() { val thread = AtomicReference<String>() orders.onFind { thread.set(Thread.currentThread().name) } val request = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(5)) // 4. arrive on a non-blocking thread, .thenReturn(OrderRequest("order-42")) // as the real server does StepVerifier.create(page.view(request)).expectNextCount(1).verifyComplete() assertThat(thread.get()).startsWith("boundedElastic-") }

lab.title: A reactive front for the old stock book
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail. StockBook is the blocking stock book, PriceList is the non-blocking price list, and ShopStock puts a reactive front on both. Read the failure of the stockValue test: it's the block() message from the last section.
Write loavesLeft(shop): wrap stock.loavesLeft(shop) so that it runs only when subscribed, on Schedulers.boundedElastic().
Write loavesLeftIn(shops): the counts for all the shops in the input order, with at most 4 stock-book calls at a time. Reuse loavesLeft.
Fix stockValue without block(). Then run the tests until all five pass, and run them once more: the concurrency test must pass every time.
hints: If the boundedElastic test reports the thread Test worker, the call ran on the thread that subscribed: subscribeOn is missing.
If loavesLeftIn peaks at 1 call in flight, your subscribeOn sits on the outer Flux, or loavesLeft lacks it. Each inner Mono needs its own.
If it peaks at 20, you used flatMap or flatMapSequential without the concurrency argument (the default is 256).
If the order test fails, use flatMapSequential(this::loavesLeft, 4) from Transforming streams: it runs inners concurrently and emits in source order.
lab.done: All five tests in ShopStockTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Wrap a blocking client from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. archive.fetchRecipe(id) is a blocking call to the bakery's old recipe archive. Write Mono<Recipe> recipe(String id) that never blocks the subscriber's thread, and Flux<Recipe> recipes(List<String> ids) that runs at most 8 calls at once, in any order. Then compare.

answer.html: Mono<Recipe> recipe(String id) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> archive.fetchRecipe(id)) // lazy, exceptions become onError .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()); // a thread that may block } Flux<Recipe> recipes(List<String> ids) { return Flux.fromIterable(ids) .flatMap(this::recipe, 8); // each inner has its own subscribeOn }

alt.html: fun recipe(id: String): Mono<Recipe> = Mono.fromCallable { archive.fetchRecipe(id) } // lazy, exceptions become onError .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // a thread that may block fun recipes(ids: List<String>): Flux<Recipe> = Flux.fromIterable(ids) .flatMap({ recipe(it) }, 8) // each inner has its own subscribeOn

recap: Without a scheduler, a chain runs on the thread that subscribed; after a timer or a non-blocking client, it runs on whatever thread delivered the item.
publishOn moves the operators after it to one worker of a scheduler. subscribeOn moves the subscription, and so the source, wherever you write it; with several, the one nearest the source wins.
Wrap blocking calls as Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()), with subscribeOn on each inner Mono, and cap the fan-out with flatMap's concurrency.
On JDK 21 or later, -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true (Reactor 3.6+) runs boundedElastic tasks on virtual threads.
block() throws on parallel and single threads and belongs only at the edges. Inside a chain, compose with flatMap.

The limit: Reactor only catches block() itself, and only on threads it marked. A blocking call on the wrong thread throws nothing, and Mono.just stubs hide even block(), so tests must deliver items on a non-blocking thread.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "What's the difference between publishOn and subscribeOn, and which one do I use to call our old stock database from a reactive chain?" Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: Both move work to a scheduler's thread, but in different directions. publishOn sits in the stream of items: everything after it runs on the new thread, and everything before it is unchanged. subscribeOn changes the thread on which the subscription travels up to the source, so the source itself runs there, no matter where in the chain you write it; if there are several, the one nearest the source wins. For a blocking database call you want the call itself to run on a thread that may block, so you wrap it as Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.loavesLeft(shop)) and add subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) to that Mono. If you make many calls in a flatMap, each inner Mono needs its own subscribeOn, and you cap the concurrency at the number of connections the database allows.

deeper.html:
ParallelFlux. For CPU-heavy work on many items, flux.parallel(4).runOn(Schedulers.parallel()).map(this::render).sequential() splits the stream into 4 rails, runs each rail on its own parallel worker, and merges them back. Without runOn, the rails exist but share one thread. sequential() merges the rails as items finish, so the original order is lost.

Tuning the shared schedulers. System properties set the sizes before the Schedulers class loads: reactor.schedulers.defaultPoolSize for parallel, reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticSize (threads) and reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticQueueSize (queued tasks) for boundedElastic. Prefer a dedicated Schedulers.newBoundedElastic(20, 1_000, "stock") per slow dependency. It works like the bulkhead from the executors track, a wall between pools: one slow dependency can only use up its own threads. Dispose it on shutdown.

publishOn prefetch. publishOn requests 256 items up front and then tops up, so it also changes the demand the source sees. publishOn(scheduler, 32) lowers that. The next lesson looks at demand in detail.

Coroutines on a Reactor scheduler. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor has Schedulers.boundedElastic().asCoroutineDispatcher(), so coroutine code can share the same threads as the Reactor parts of a program.
